title: Reharmonization
intro: Jazz players rarely play a tune's chords as written. Reharmonization swaps chords for others that share their function or their guide tones, adding colour and surprise without losing the song.

blocks.text: A dominant seventh and the dominant seventh a tritone away share their tritone: G7 (G B D F) and D♭7 (D♭ F A♭ C♭=B) both contain B and F. Either can resolve to C, so Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 can become Dm7–D♭7–Cmaj7, giving a chromatic bass line D–D♭–C. The substituted chord's natural tensions are the altered tensions of the original (A♭ is ♭9 of G7).

widget.title: ii–V–I with and without tritone substitution

items: Any dominant can be preceded by its ii: G7 becomes Dm7–G7, and a secondary dominant A7 becomes Em7–A7.
The backdoor ii–V uses iv–♭VII7 instead: Fm7–B♭7–Cmaj7. B♭7 resolves up a whole step to C, borrowing from the parallel minor.
Diminished passing chords: C–C♯°7–Dm7, the °7 acting as vii°7/ii.

blocks.text: John Coltrane's 'Giant Steps' (1959) divides the octave into three major thirds and moves the tonic among them (B, G, E♭), each approached by its own V7: Bmaj7 D7 Gmaj7 B♭7 E♭maj7 …. Coltrane also used these 'Coltrane substitutions' over an ordinary ii–V–I, which takes an improviser through three keys in two bars.

In modal jazz ('So What', 'Impressions') a chord holds for many bars and the mode, not the progression, is the material. Pianists voice such chords in fourths, which avoids the strong pull of chords built in thirds: Bill Evans's 'So What' voicing for D Dorian is E–A–D–G–B (three fourths and a major third) over a D bass, and McCoy Tyner built whole solos on stacked fourths.

Take a simple standard and reharmonize one ii–V at a time: first tritone-substitute the V, then add a related ii before it (Dm7–A♭m7–D♭7–C), then try the backdoor. Keep the melody note on top and check it fits each new chord (it should be a chord tone or an available tension).

blocks.title: Tritone sub
blocks.text: What is the tritone substitute for E7, and what does it resolve to?
solution: A tritone above E is B♭: B♭7 (B♭ D F A♭). It shares the tritone G♯/A♭–D with E7 and resolves, like E7, to A (or Am).

blocks.title: Backdoor
blocks.text: Write a backdoor ii–V to E♭ major.
solution: The backdoor uses iv7–♭VII7 of the key: iv in E♭ is A♭m, ♭VII is D♭. A♭m7–D♭7–E♭maj7.

blocks.text: Sources: Levine, M. (1995). The Jazz Theory Book. Sher Music; Porter, L. (1998). John Coltrane: His Life and Music. University of Michigan Press; Demsey, D. (1991). Chromatic third relations in the music of John Coltrane. Annual Review of Jazz Studies 5.
